title: Largest Perimeter Triangle
approach_name: Check largest sorted triples
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest perimeter of a non-degenerate triangle that can be formed from three array values, or zero if impossible.
Idea: Sort the side lengths and inspect triples from largest to smallest; the first triple with `a+b>c` has the maximum possible perimeter.
Technique and why it applies: Descending triples let the method return the largest perimeter as soon as the triangle inequality succeeds.
Invariant: For a descending triple `a >= b >= c`, once `b+c>a` holds it forms a triangle, and no later triple can have a larger perimeter.
Edge cases: Triples with equality fail the strict triangle inequality; fewer than three usable sides return zero.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by O(n) checks; auxiliary space depends on the sorting implementation.
complexity_reason: Descending triples let the method return the largest perimeter as soon as the triangle inequality succeeds.

title: Largest Perimeter Triangle
approach_name: Check largest sorted triples
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the largest perimeter of a non-degenerate triangle that can be formed from three array values, or zero if impossible.
Idea: Sort the side lengths and inspect triples from largest to smallest; the first triple with `a+b>c` has the maximum possible perimeter.
Technique and why it applies: Descending triples let the method return the largest perimeter as soon as the triangle inequality succeeds.
Invariant: For a descending triple `a >= b >= c`, once `b+c>a` holds it forms a triangle, and no later triple can have a larger perimeter.
Edge cases: Triples with equality fail the strict triangle inequality; fewer than three usable sides return zero.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), followed by O(n) checks; auxiliary space depends on the sorting implementation.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public int largestPerimeter(int[] nums){Arrays.sort(nums);for(int i=nums.length-1;i>=2;i--)if(nums[i-1]+nums[i-2]>nums[i])return nums[i]+nums[i-1]+nums[i-2];return 0;} }
complexity_reason: Descending triples let the method return the largest perimeter as soon as the triangle inequality succeeds.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
approach_name: Fill output from largest square downward
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the squares of a nondecreasing array in nondecreasing order.
Idea: Use left and right pointers at the smallest and largest input values, compare their squares, and fill the output from the final index backward.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing endpoint magnitudes avoids sorting the squares after a linear two-pointer pass.
Invariant: At each step, the larger remaining absolute endpoint has the largest remaining square and belongs at the current rightmost output position.
Edge cases: Negative values can have large squares; equal magnitudes may be taken from either end; empty input yields empty output.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
complexity_reason: Comparing endpoint magnitudes avoids sorting the squares after a linear two-pointer pass.

title: Squares of a Sorted Array
approach_name: Fill output from largest square downward
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the squares of a nondecreasing array in nondecreasing order.
Idea: Use left and right pointers at the smallest and largest input values, compare their squares, and fill the output from the final index backward.
Technique and why it applies: Comparing endpoint magnitudes avoids sorting the squares after a linear two-pointer pass.
Invariant: At each step, the larger remaining absolute endpoint has the largest remaining square and belongs at the current rightmost output position.
Edge cases: Negative values can have large squares; equal magnitudes may be taken from either end; empty input yields empty output.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(n) output space.
code: class Solution { public int[] sortedSquares(int[] nums){int n=nums.length;int[]out=new int[n];int l=0,r=n-1;for(int i=n-1;i>=0;i--)if(Math.abs(nums[l])>Math.abs(nums[r])){out[i]=nums[l]*nums[l];l++;}else{out[i]=nums[r]*nums[r];r--;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Comparing endpoint magnitudes avoids sorting the squares after a linear two-pointer pass.

title: Sum of Even Numbers After Queries
approach_name: Maintain the even sum incrementally
notes:
Task and constraints: For each [value,index] query, add value to nums[index] and return the sum of even values after that update.
Idea: Compute the initial sum of even values; for each query subtract the old value if even, apply the update, add the new value if even, and save the total.
Technique and why it applies: Removing the old even contribution and adding the new one maintains the even sum incrementally per query.
Invariant: The running sum always equals the sum of even elements in the currently updated array.
Edge cases: Negative even values are still even; each query updates one index; query order matters.
Complexity: O(n+q) time and O(q) output space, with O(1) extra working space.
complexity_reason: Removing the old even contribution and adding the new one maintains the even sum incrementally per query.

title: Sum of Even Numbers After Queries
approach_name: Maintain the even sum incrementally
notes:
Task and constraints: For each [value,index] query, add value to nums[index] and return the sum of even values after that update.
Idea: Compute the initial sum of even values; for each query subtract the old value if even, apply the update, add the new value if even, and save the total.
Technique and why it applies: Removing the old even contribution and adding the new one maintains the even sum incrementally per query.
Invariant: The running sum always equals the sum of even elements in the currently updated array.
Edge cases: Negative even values are still even; each query updates one index; query order matters.
Complexity: O(n+q) time and O(q) output space, with O(1) extra working space.
code: class Solution { public int[] sumEvenAfterQueries(int[] nums,int[][] queries){int total=0;for(int x:nums)if(x%2==0)total+=x;int[]out=new int[queries.length];for(int i=0;i<queries.length;i++){int v=queries[i][0],idx=queries[i][1];if(nums[idx]%2==0)total-=nums[idx];nums[idx]+=v;if(nums[idx]%2==0)total+=nums[idx];out[i]=total;}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Removing the old even contribution and adding the new one maintains the even sum incrementally per query.

title: Add to Array-Form of Integer
approach_name: Add from the least significant digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Treat the digit array as a nonnegative integer and return its sum with k in digit-array form.
Idea: Add `k` from the least significant end of the digit array, carrying tens into the next digit and collecting result digits in reverse order.
Technique and why it applies: Right-to-left digit addition handles arbitrary carry without converting the whole number to a machine integer.
Invariant: After processing each position, the carry and collected digits represent the low-order portion of the sum already handled.
Edge cases: The digit array may have leading digits beyond `k`; remaining carry is emitted; reverse the collected digits before returning.
Complexity: O(n+digits(k)) time and O(n+digits(k)) output space.
complexity_reason: Right-to-left digit addition handles arbitrary carry without converting the whole number to a machine integer.

title: Add to Array-Form of Integer
approach_name: Add from the least significant digit
notes:
Task and constraints: Treat the digit array as a nonnegative integer and return its sum with k in digit-array form.
Idea: Add `k` from the least significant end of the digit array, carrying tens into the next digit and collecting result digits in reverse order.
Technique and why it applies: Right-to-left digit addition handles arbitrary carry without converting the whole number to a machine integer.
Invariant: After processing each position, the carry and collected digits represent the low-order portion of the sum already handled.
Edge cases: The digit array may have leading digits beyond `k`; remaining carry is emitted; reverse the collected digits before returning.
Complexity: O(n+digits(k)) time and O(n+digits(k)) output space.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<Integer> addToArrayForm(int[] num,int k){List<Integer>out=new ArrayList<>();int i=num.length-1;while(i>=0||k>0){if(i>=0)k+=num[i--];out.add(k%10);k/=10;}Collections.reverse(out);return out;} }
complexity_reason: Right-to-left digit addition handles arbitrary carry without converting the whole number to a machine integer.

title: Find the Town Judge
approach_name: Count trust in and out degrees
notes:
Task and constraints: In a town of n people, find the judge who trusts nobody and is trusted by everyone else, or return -1.
Idea: Count trust edges entering and leaving each person; a judge has `n-1` incoming edges and zero outgoing edges.
Technique and why it applies: In-degree and out-degree conditions encode both judge requirements in a single candidate check.
Invariant: For each person, `in-degree - out-degree` equals `n-1` exactly for someone trusted by all others and trusting nobody.
Edge cases: For n=1, the sole person qualifies if there are no trust edges; otherwise return -1 when no candidate matches.
Complexity: O(n+trust edges) time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: In-degree and out-degree conditions encode both judge requirements in a single candidate check.

title: Find the Town Judge
approach_name: Count trust in and out degrees
notes:
Task and constraints: In a town of n people, find the judge who trusts nobody and is trusted by everyone else, or return -1.
Idea: Count trust edges entering and leaving each person; a judge has `n-1` incoming edges and zero outgoing edges.
Technique and why it applies: In-degree and out-degree conditions encode both judge requirements in a single candidate check.
Invariant: For each person, `in-degree - out-degree` equals `n-1` exactly for someone trusted by all others and trusting nobody.
Edge cases: For n=1, the sole person qualifies if there are no trust edges; otherwise return -1 when no candidate matches.
Complexity: O(n+trust edges) time and O(n) space.
code: class Solution { public int findJudge(int n,int[][] trust){int[]score=new int[n+1];for(int[]e:trust){score[e[0]]--;score[e[1]]++;}for(int i=1;i<=n;i++)if(score[i]==n-1)return i;return -1;} }
complexity_reason: In-degree and out-degree conditions encode both judge requirements in a single candidate check.

title: Find Common Characters
approach_name: Intersect character frequencies
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all lowercase characters that appear in every word, including duplicates according to the minimum frequency.
Idea: Count letters in the first word, then take the per-character minimum with each later word's frequency; emit each letter that many times.
Technique and why it applies: Taking minimum letter frequencies across words gives exactly the multiset intersection required.
Invariant: The working frequency array after processing a prefix of words stores the minimum frequency seen for every character in all those words.
Edge cases: Repeated common letters must be emitted multiple times; lowercase English letters bound the frequency array to 26 slots.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) auxiliary alphabet space apart from the output.
complexity_reason: Taking minimum letter frequencies across words gives exactly the multiset intersection required.

title: Find Common Characters
approach_name: Intersect character frequencies
notes:
Task and constraints: Return all lowercase characters that appear in every word, including duplicates according to the minimum frequency.
Idea: Count letters in the first word, then take the per-character minimum with each later word's frequency; emit each letter that many times.
Technique and why it applies: Taking minimum letter frequencies across words gives exactly the multiset intersection required.
Invariant: The working frequency array after processing a prefix of words stores the minimum frequency seen for every character in all those words.
Edge cases: Repeated common letters must be emitted multiple times; lowercase English letters bound the frequency array to 26 slots.
Complexity: O(total characters) time and O(1) auxiliary alphabet space apart from the output.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<String> commonChars(String[] words){int[]min=new int[26];Arrays.fill(min,Integer.MAX_VALUE);for(String w:words){int[]c=new int[26];for(char x:w.toCharArray())c[x-'a']++;for(int i=0;i<26;i++)min[i]=Math.min(min[i],c[i]);}List<String>out=new ArrayList<>();for(int i=0;i<26;i++)for(int j=0;j<min[i];j++)out.add(String.valueOf((char)('a'+i)));return out;} }
complexity_reason: Taking minimum letter frequencies across words gives exactly the multiset intersection required.

title: Maximize Sum Of Array After K Negations
approach_name: Flip negatives then the smallest absolute value
notes:
Task and constraints: After exactly k sign flips, return the maximum possible array sum.
Idea: Sort or otherwise process negative values first, flip negative values while moves remain, then spend any odd leftover flip on the value with smallest absolute magnitude.
Technique and why it applies: Using flips on negatives first and then the smallest absolute value maximizes the final total.
Invariant: Flipping a negative increases the sum; after all useful negative flips, only the least costly absolute value can minimize the loss from an odd remaining flip.
Edge cases: Exactly k flips are required; flipping the same element twice cancels; zero absorbs any leftover odd flip without reducing the sum.
Complexity: O(n log n) time if sorting is used and O(1) or O(n) extra space depending on implementation.
complexity_reason: Using flips on negatives first and then the smallest absolute value maximizes the final total.

title: Maximize Sum Of Array After K Negations
approach_name: Flip negatives then the smallest absolute value
notes:
Task and constraints: After exactly k sign flips, return the maximum possible array sum.
Idea: Sort or otherwise process negative values first, flip negative values while moves remain, then spend any odd leftover flip on the value with smallest absolute magnitude.
Technique and why it applies: Using flips on negatives first and then the smallest absolute value maximizes the final total.
Invariant: Flipping a negative increases the sum; after all useful negative flips, only the least costly absolute value can minimize the loss from an odd remaining flip.
Edge cases: Exactly k flips are required; flipping the same element twice cancels; zero absorbs any leftover odd flip without reducing the sum.
Complexity: O(n log n) time if sorting is used and O(1) or O(n) extra space depending on implementation.
code: class Solution { public int largestSumAfterKNegations(int[] nums,int k){Arrays.sort(nums);for(int i=0;i<nums.length&&k>0;i++)if(nums[i]<0){nums[i]=-nums[i];k--;}int sum=0,min=Integer.MAX_VALUE;for(int x:nums){sum+=x;min=Math.min(min,Math.abs(x));}if(k%2==1)sum-=2*min;return sum;} }
complexity_reason: Using flips on negatives first and then the smallest absolute value maximizes the final total.

title: Complement of Base 10 Integer
approach_name: XOR against a same-width bit mask
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the bitwise complement of a nonnegative integer, ignoring leading zero bits.
Idea: Build a bit mask containing ones across the number's significant binary width and XOR it with the number.
Technique and why it applies: A width-matched all-ones mask complements only significant bits and avoids unwanted leading bits.
Invariant: The mask has no leading zero bits and flips each significant bit while leaving no extra high-order bits in the result.
Edge cases: For input zero, its representation is one zero bit, so the complement should be one; handle this case explicitly if needed.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: A width-matched all-ones mask complements only significant bits and avoids unwanted leading bits.

title: Complement of Base 10 Integer
approach_name: XOR against a same-width bit mask
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the bitwise complement of a nonnegative integer, ignoring leading zero bits.
Idea: Build a bit mask containing ones across the number's significant binary width and XOR it with the number.
Technique and why it applies: A width-matched all-ones mask complements only significant bits and avoids unwanted leading bits.
Invariant: The mask has no leading zero bits and flips each significant bit while leaving no extra high-order bits in the result.
Edge cases: For input zero, its representation is one zero bit, so the complement should be one; handle this case explicitly if needed.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.
code: class Solution { public int bitwiseComplement(int n){int mask=1;while(mask<n)mask=(mask<<1)|1;return n^mask;} }
complexity_reason: A width-matched all-ones mask complements only significant bits and avoids unwanted leading bits.

title: Partition Array Into Three Parts With Equal Sum
approach_name: Find two target-sum prefixes
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if an array can be split into three nonempty contiguous parts with equal sums.
Idea: Require the total sum to be divisible by three, scan prefix sums, and identify two target-sum segments while leaving a nonempty third segment.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-sum targets find two equal-sum cut points without trying every possible pair of cuts.
Invariant: The first completed target segment and second completed target segment consume distinct indices, and the remaining suffix must form the third target sum.
Edge cases: The array must be long enough for three nonempty parts; if the total is not divisible by three, return false immediately.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Prefix-sum targets find two equal-sum cut points without trying every possible pair of cuts.

title: Partition Array Into Three Parts With Equal Sum
approach_name: Find two target-sum prefixes
notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if an array can be split into three nonempty contiguous parts with equal sums.
Idea: Require the total sum to be divisible by three, scan prefix sums, and identify two target-sum segments while leaving a nonempty third segment.
Technique and why it applies: Prefix-sum targets find two equal-sum cut points without trying every possible pair of cuts.
Invariant: The first completed target segment and second completed target segment consume distinct indices, and the remaining suffix must form the third target sum.
Edge cases: The array must be long enough for three nonempty parts; if the total is not divisible by three, return false immediately.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
code: class Solution { public boolean canThreePartsEqualSum(int[] arr){int total=0;for(int x:arr)total+=x;if(total%3!=0)return false;int target=total/3,parts=0,cur=0;for(int i=0;i<arr.length-1;i++){cur+=arr[i];if(cur==target){parts++;cur=0;if(parts==2)return true;}}return false;} }
complexity_reason: Prefix-sum targets find two equal-sum cut points without trying every possible pair of cuts.

title: Binary Prefix Divisible By 5
approach_name: Maintain prefix remainder
notes:
Task and constraints: For every prefix of a binary array, return whether its represented integer is divisible by 5.
Idea: Update the prefix remainder as `(remainder*2 + bit) % 5` and record whether it equals zero after each bit.
Technique and why it applies: Maintaining only the modulo-five remainder avoids constructing increasingly large binary prefix values.
Invariant: The stored remainder equals the integer represented by the processed prefix modulo five, even when the prefix itself is very large.
Edge cases: Each prefix contributes one boolean; reducing modulo five prevents integer growth and works for leading zero bits.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from the O(n) result.
complexity_reason: Maintaining only the modulo-five remainder avoids constructing increasingly large binary prefix values.

title: Binary Prefix Divisible By 5
approach_name: Maintain prefix remainder
notes:
Task and constraints: For every prefix of a binary array, return whether its represented integer is divisible by 5.
Idea: Update the prefix remainder as `(remainder*2 + bit) % 5` and record whether it equals zero after each bit.
Technique and why it applies: Maintaining only the modulo-five remainder avoids constructing increasingly large binary prefix values.
Invariant: The stored remainder equals the integer represented by the processed prefix modulo five, even when the prefix itself is very large.
Edge cases: Each prefix contributes one boolean; reducing modulo five prevents integer growth and works for leading zero bits.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space apart from the O(n) result.
code:
import java.util.*;
class Solution { public List<Boolean> prefixesDivBy5(int[] nums){List<Boolean>out=new ArrayList<>();int rem=0;for(int b:nums){rem=(rem*2+b)%5;out.add(rem==0);}return out;} }
complexity_reason: Maintaining only the modulo-five remainder avoids constructing increasingly large binary prefix values.
